parts.title: Understanding Software Applications
parts.question: What should we build, who needs it, and what work will building it require?
parts.intro: Before asking an AI assistant for code, learn to describe the thing you want people to use. This part helps you connect a real problem to a manageable application, then see the work beyond its screens.

project.title: Create a clear application brief
project.summary: Make a short planning document that another person could use without guessing your intentions. Describe the users, their difficulty, the smallest helpful version, and evidence that it works. Ask an AI assistant to point out unanswered questions rather than build anything yet.
steps: Name a specific group of users and explain their problem and present workaround.
Describe the application in one sentence and choose a type, explaining the trade-off.
Write one short user journey and identify the essential features that support it.
Separate first-version features from explicitly postponed ideas.
Write three user stories with testable acceptance criteria, including an invalid input and a permission failure.
Record measurable quality expectations, constraints, assumptions, and unresolved questions.
Plan a small build-test-feedback loop and review the brief for contradictions.

glossary.definition: Computer instructions and the information used with them.
A particular set of instructions that can be executed.
A running instance of a program.
Software arranged to help someone accomplish a purpose.
Applications, infrastructure, information, people, and procedures working together.
A capability that helps a user achieve a specific result.
The processor that carries out machine instructions.
Fast working memory used while programs execute.
Storage intended to retain information beyond the current execution.
Connections through which computers exchange information.
An application accessed through a browser.
A defined way for software to request another component’s capabilities.
A sequence of actions leading to a user’s goal.
A short account of who needs a capability and why.
Observable conditions used to judge whether behaviour is delivered.
An expectation about how well the application must work.
A boundary the solution must respect.
An unconfirmed belief used in planning.
The work included in a particular effort or release.
The smallest coherent release that solves a real problem.
The recurring work of planning, design, implementation, testing, release, and maintenance.
Making software usable through different abilities and interaction methods.

chapters.title: What Software and Applications Are
chapters.question: When you ask an AI assistant for an application, what pieces should you expect it to create?
chapters.summary: An application is more than the screen someone clicks. Its instructions, information, and computing resources must work together to deliver complete features.

sections.heading: Four useful names
paragraphs: Software is the broad name for computer instructions and the information used with them. A program is a particular collection of instructions that can run. Once a program is executing, the operating system manages that running instance as a process. You can launch two processes from the same program, just as you can open the same document in two separate windows.

An application puts software to work for a person's purpose, such as organising appointments. It may contain several cooperating programs. A system is the larger arrangement around it: applications, computers, networks, records, people, and procedures. A booking system therefore includes more than a booking app; it may also include staff who resolve cancellations. These names describe different viewpoints, not competing labels.

sections.heading: The interface is only the visible part
paragraphs: A screen gives someone a way to communicate with software, but it cannot show everything happening underneath. A task form may depend on another program to check rules and a database to remember the result. Those pieces can run in different places. Closing the screen does not necessarily stop the programs serving other users.

This matters when reviewing AI-generated work. A convincing page can be a demonstration with invented records rather than a working application. Ask where each action goes, which rules are applied, and how the result is kept. You do not need the implementation vocabulary immediately; you do need to distinguish a useful-looking surface from a complete capability.

sections.heading: Instructions operate on data
paragraphs: Instructions specify what happens and in what order. For a new task, the sequence might check the submitted title, associate the task with the signed-in person, save it, and report the result. Computers do not fill in missing product decisions with human common sense. An unspecified rule is a decision somebody, including an AI tool, will make for you.

Data is the information those instructions use. A title typed into a form is input data; a stored task is saved data; a count of unfinished tasks is derived data. The same information can move through several forms. Notice which pieces come from the person and which the application must determine itself, especially ownership and calculated values.

sections.heading: The resources that make execution possible
paragraphs: A processor, often called a CPU, performs the low-level work. Memory, or RAM, provides fast working space while programs operate. Persistent storage keeps information beyond the current execution. A network allows programs on separate computers to exchange messages. Even a small feature needs these resources somewhere, although a hosting provider may operate many of them for you.

These resources have different jobs and limits. A busy processor can delay calculations; too little memory can stop a program; a broken network can prevent a save. Persistent storage does not mean indestructible storage: disks and services can fail, so important information still needs appropriate protection and backups. Knowing the categories helps you ask more precise questions about failures.

sections.heading: Temporary state is not a saved record
paragraphs: Imagine writing a shopping list on a reusable board and then wiping it. That resembles information kept only in working memory. A browser page may display a task held in a JavaScript variable, yet lose it as soon as the page reloads. Server memory has a similar limitation when the server process stops or restarts.

Saving information durably is a separate operation. Some browser storage survives reloads, but remains tied to that browser and can be cleared. A server-side database can provide a shared, persistent record accessible from different devices. To check a save, do more than watch a row appear: reload, sign in again, or read the record from another device.

sections.heading: Build complete feature slices
paragraphs: A feature is a useful capability, such as completing a task. It normally crosses several layers: a control on the screen, instructions that enforce rules, and a stored change. Treat those layers as one slice of useful behaviour. A checkbox with no saved effect is not a completed feature, even when its animation looks polished.

Building one slice at a time gives you something meaningful to test. First make one task save correctly through every layer; then expand the application. This is usually easier to assess than generating every screen before connecting any of them. Include the failure path in the slice, because people need to know whether an action actually succeeded.

chapters.keyIdea: A feature is complete only when its interface, rules, and saved data work together.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard includes accounts, task creation, editing, deletion, due dates, completion, and an ordered personal task list. Its browser interface communicates with backend instructions, while a database retains accounts and tasks. Each visible action must connect these pieces rather than merely change the page.

walkthrough.title: Follow one completion checkbox
steps: Tick an unfinished task and show that the action is waiting.
Send the task identifier and requested change to the backend.
Check the session and whether the task belongs to that person.
Save the new completion value in persistent storage.
Report success or failure, then reload to confirm the saved outcome.

mistakes: Calling a feature finished because its button responds visually.
Confusing a temporary list on screen with durable, shared storage.
aiMistakes: AI may generate sample arrays instead of persistence; reload the page and inspect where records are stored.
AI may omit ownership checks; use two test accounts and attempt the same change from the wrong one.
tryIt: Choose a familiar app and list five features, then name the interface action, rule, and stored information behind each.
Create a record in a demo, refresh it, and explain what that does and does not prove about storage.

check.q: How does an application differ from a program?
check.a: An application serves a user goal and may coordinate several runnable programs.

check.q: Why can a task disappear after a refresh?
check.a: It may have existed only in page memory rather than being saved and loaded again.

chapters.title: Different Types of Applications
chapters.question: Which kind of application best fits your users rather than simply being easiest for a tool to generate?
chapters.summary: Application types differ in where they execute, how people obtain updates, and which device capabilities they can use. Choose from user needs and operating responsibilities, including software that has no screen.

sections.heading: Browser-based applications
paragraphs: A web application opens at an address in a browser. People usually need no separate installation, and the same service can reach phones, tablets, and laptops. Deploying a new frontend makes it available when users next load the updated version, although caching and already-open pages can affect timing. This makes web applications a practical starting point for many small products.

The browser also creates boundaries. Access to hardware and background activity varies by browser and operating system. A web application often depends on a connection for its main work. Do not assume that fitting a page onto a phone gives it every ability of an installed phone app. Check the particular feature on the actual devices your users have.

sections.heading: Installed mobile and desktop applications
paragraphs: Mobile apps are installed on phones or tablets, often through an app store. Native development uses tools tailored to one platform, while cross-platform frameworks share more code between platforms. Either approach can still require platform-specific testing and adjustments. Device integration, notifications, and offline behaviour may favour mobile development, but store submission and update distribution add work.

Desktop applications run on computers such as Windows PCs or Macs. They can suit large files, extensive keyboard work, or intensive local processing. Some package web technologies inside a desktop shell. Installation does not remove maintenance: you may support several operating systems and multiple old versions at once. Unlike a centrally hosted service, you cannot assume everyone installs an update immediately.

sections.heading: Command lines and invisible software
paragraphs: A command-line application receives typed instructions in a terminal and returns text or files. It can be excellent for repeatable technical work and automation, even though it offers no buttons. The best interface depends on the audience: a developer may prefer one short command, whereas an occasional nontechnical user may need a guided form and visible choices.

Other software works without direct interaction. Background services handle ongoing or deferred work; scheduled jobs start at specified times; automation scripts connect repetitive steps across systems. An API gives other software a defined way to use a capability. These categories can overlap. A daily reminder may be started by a schedule, processed by a worker, and delivered through an email provider's API.

sections.heading: Where it runs and who operates it
paragraphs: Installed software executes on a user's device, while hosted software runs on computers operated for the service. Many applications combine both: a browser displays the interface and a hosted backend stores records. A cloud service is still software running on physical computers; the phrase describes an operating arrangement, not freedom from resource limits or responsibility.

Offline and local-first designs prioritise work that can continue without a connection. That can be valuable, but synchronising later introduces questions about conflicting edits, lost devices, and duplicate actions. Decide which actions must work offline and what happens on reconnection. Merely saving the application's files on a phone does not make all its data and operations available offline.

sections.heading: Progressive web applications and practical trade-offs
paragraphs: A progressive web application, or PWA, adds selected app-like abilities to a web application. A service worker can keep application resources available and help support offline behaviour. On supported platforms, people may add it to their home screen. These possibilities are useful, but installation, notifications, and background features are not identical across every browser and device.

Compare options using the actual requirements: audience, distribution, hardware access, connection quality, performance, development effort, updates, and ongoing cost. A simple hosted app can reduce first-version complexity, while introducing hosting and network dependence. An installed app can improve local capabilities, while increasing release work. Write down what you gain and give up rather than declaring one type universally superior.

sections.heading: Keep trust boundaries visible
paragraphs: Code and information shipped to a person's device can be inspected. A secret embedded in a web bundle or installed client is not protected merely because the interface does not show it. Credentials for privileged external services belong on a backend you control. That backend must also enforce important permissions, regardless of which kind of client calls it.

Separating reusable rules and data behind an API can make later expansion easier. A web interface and a future mobile interface can ask the same backend to create tasks. This does not mean you must build every interface now. Choose the smallest arrangement that meets present needs, while avoiding shortcuts that would expose secrets or make another client impossible to support safely.

chapters.keyIdea: Choose an application type by its users, environment, and maintenance demands, not by fashion.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard starts as a responsive web application because people need their task list on different devices without installation. Its shared backend keeps rules and records consistent. Reliable offline editing and app-store distribution are deliberately separate decisions rather than assumed benefits.

walkthrough.title: Choose a first home for Taskboard
steps: Describe users switching between a work laptop and a personal phone.
Check whether their essential actions require specialist hardware or reliable offline operation.
Compare a responsive web app with mobile and desktop alternatives.
Choose a web first version and record its connection requirement.
Place private credentials and enforceable rules on the backend, allowing future clients to reuse them.

mistakes: Picking mobile because the word app sounds like a phone product.
Promising offline support without planning synchronisation or conflicts.
aiMistakes: AI may embed an API secret in downloadable client code; inspect configuration and built-client usage.
AI may promise unsupported PWA capabilities; test the exact platform before accepting the design.
tryIt: Compare two application types for a local fieldworker who often has no signal.
Identify one background service and one scheduled job in a product you use.

check.q: Is a scheduled job the same as a screen?
check.a: No; it is work triggered by a timetable and may have no user interface.

check.q: Why are hosted updates simpler to distribute?
check.a: The operator can change the central service rather than depend on every user updating an installation.

chapters.title: From a Problem to Application Requirements
chapters.question: How can you make sure a polished application solves something people actually need?
chapters.summary: Requirements turn an appealing idea into explicit decisions about users, behaviour, quality, and scope. A small useful release needs clear completion criteria, not merely a long feature list.

sections.heading: Begin with people and their workaround
paragraphs: Choose a recognisable group of users rather than everybody. Ask what they are trying to accomplish, what interrupts them, and how they handle it today. Their existing solution may be paper, a spreadsheet, several messages, or memory. That workaround tells you what a new application must improve enough to justify learning and using it.

Write a problem statement before describing technology. For example, independent workers may miss small commitments because dates are scattered across notebooks and messages. This identifies people, difficulty, and consequence without assuming a calendar, chatbot, or social feed is required. Ask potential users about a recent real incident; specific experiences reveal more than asking whether they like your proposed idea.

sections.heading: Map a journey to an outcome
paragraphs: A user journey is a short sequence of actions that reaches a goal. For planning tomorrow, someone might open their tasks, inspect upcoming dates, add a forgotten item, and finish knowing what matters next. Describe the journey in ordinary language. Avoid starting with a catalogue of screens, because a screen is useful only as part of someone's work.

Look for missing steps and unnecessary additions. If the journey requires seeing dates together, a create-task form alone is insufficient. If nothing involves collaboration, team invitations may not belong in the first version. Journeys also expose return visits and recovery: what happens when the person comes back later, has no tasks, or discovers a mistake in something already entered?

sections.heading: Turn capabilities into purposeful stories
paragraphs: A feature names something the application lets people do. A user story adds who needs it and why. You could write that a busy worker needs tasks ordered by due date so that the next commitment is easy to identify. The purpose helps resolve details without treating every design choice as equally important. Stories invite discussion; they are not automatically complete specifications.

Keep the user's goal separate from an implementation preference. A request for a particular button placement may conceal a need for faster repeated entry. Ask what result matters before committing to the layout. Connect each first-version feature to a journey or requirement. If you cannot explain whom it helps and how, it may be an attractive distraction rather than essential scope.

sections.heading: Make completion testable
paragraphs: Acceptance criteria describe observable conditions that show a story is delivered. A useful pattern states the starting situation, the action, and the expected outcome. For date ordering, specify how undated tasks appear and what happens to equal dates. These details prevent different people, or an AI assistant, from implementing incompatible interpretations of the same sentence.

Include rejection and recovery as well as success. An empty title should receive a clear response and create no task. A person should not access another person's record. A failed save should not discard the entered text. Phrase criteria so somebody can demonstrate them with concrete examples. Words such as intuitive, fast, or secure need more detail before they can guide a meaningful check.

sections.heading: Record quality, limits, and uncertainty
paragraphs: Functional requirements say what the application does. Quality requirements describe how well it must do it: for example, an explicit response-time target under stated conditions, keyboard operation, and private records. Security and accessibility belong here from the start. They influence design and testing rather than being optional decoration after feature work is finished.

Constraints are boundaries such as a fixed budget, supported devices, or an agreed technology. Assumptions are beliefs you are using without confirmation, such as users usually having a connection. Dependencies are things the plan relies on, such as an email service. Keep these categories visible: a fact, a limit, and a guess require different responses. Turn important unknowns into questions or small investigations.

sections.heading: Choose a minimum useful release
paragraphs: A minimum useful version solves a small real problem from beginning to end. It is not a collection of half-connected controls. For task tracking, reliable personal records may matter more than comments, attachments, or elaborate themes. Remove whole nonessential capabilities rather than removing the validation, permissions, or persistence needed for essential capabilities to work responsibly.

Write both an included list and an excluded list. The second protects the first when new ideas arrive. Record why a feature is postponed so that deliberate scope does not look like an accidental omission. Review changes against the problem and acceptance criteria. Small scope is not lack of ambition; it creates a release you can evaluate with users before investing in assumptions that may be wrong.

chapters.keyIdea: Good requirements explain whose problem matters and make successful behaviour observable.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard gives people one dependable place for personal and work tasks. Its first version supports private task management with dates and a useful ordering, while postponing team collaboration and attachments. Its brief also states quality expectations and failure behaviour rather than leaving the AI to invent them.

walkthrough.title: Specify date ordering without guesswork
steps: Name the user and explain why upcoming commitments are hard to track.
Describe opening the list and finding the next dated task.
Write a story connecting date order to that outcome.
Specify earliest dates first, undated items last, and a consistent policy for ties.
Add empty-list, invalid-date, and wrong-owner cases, then list what is out of scope.

mistakes: Treating your own feature enthusiasm as evidence of a user problem.
Calling the first version minimal by omitting safeguards rather than optional features.
aiMistakes: AI may expand scope with unrequested chat or collaboration; compare every proposal with the included list.
AI may invent unstated ordering rules; ask it to list assumptions and approve the decisions explicitly.
tryIt: Interview someone about a recent frustrating task and write a solution-free problem statement.
Write three acceptance criteria for editing a task, including a failure and a permission boundary.

check.q: How do a story and its criteria differ?
check.a: The story explains the desired capability and purpose; criteria specify checkable outcomes.

check.q: Why document excluded features?
check.a: It prevents accidental scope expansion and preserves the reasoning behind the first release.

chapters.title: The Software Development Lifecycle
chapters.question: Why does building dependable software involve much more than producing code quickly?
chapters.summary: Software development is a repeating cycle of decisions, implementation, evidence, and care. AI can accelerate parts of that cycle, but a human still owns the outcome.

sections.heading: Plan and design before implementation
paragraphs: Planning identifies the problem, intended users, priorities, scope, and practical limits. It is where you decide which result deserves effort first. A plan does not have to predict every future detail. It should be clear enough to choose a small next piece and to recognise whether completing it actually helps the people you intend to serve.

Design works out how that piece should behave and fit into the application. It includes interaction choices, data shape, responsibilities, and important boundaries, not just colours. For creating a task, design might decide where validation occurs, how an owner is determined, and how a save failure appears. These decisions are cheaper to discuss before many files depend on an accidental choice.

sections.heading: Implement, test, and release
paragraphs: Implementation turns the agreed behaviour into working code and configuration. With AI, much typing may be quick, but the result still needs review. Break work into understandable changes and connect them to requirements. A large generated change can hide unrelated decisions, making it difficult to know which part caused an error or whether essential rules were skipped.

Testing gathers evidence against expected behaviour. It includes normal use, boundaries, failures, and interactions between components. Release then makes a tested version available to its intended users. Releasing is not the same as saving a file: configuration, database changes, access, and the ability to recover from trouble may all matter. A local demonstration does not establish that the deployed version behaves correctly.

sections.heading: Maintain and learn from real use
paragraphs: Maintenance includes fixing defects, updating dependencies, addressing security issues, and improving behaviour as needs change. An application remains your responsibility after its first release. People use unexpected data and devices, services fail, and libraries evolve. Plan for observing problems and supporting users instead of assuming a successful launch ends the project.

The stages form a loop. Feedback from testing can change a design; feedback from users can change the requirements. Smaller releases shorten the time between a decision and evidence about it. An older one-pass approach tries to finish each stage before the next, while iterative work revisits them. Iteration is not an excuse for no planning; it means planning with room to learn.

sections.heading: Working is only one dimension of good
paragraphs: Correctness means the application follows its intended rules. Usability concerns whether people can understand and accomplish their work. Accessibility concerns whether people with different abilities and ways of interacting can participate. A feature may be correct when clicked with a mouse yet unusable through a keyboard or screen reader. These qualities need distinct checks.

Security protects accounts, data, and operations from misuse. Maintainability concerns how readily someone can understand and safely change the software later. A rushed solution may appear successful now while making the next change risky. Include quality expectations in the definition of done. You cannot prove that software is good solely by a screenshot, one happy-path test, or a confident explanation from its generator.

sections.heading: One person can hold several roles
paragraphs: A product role decides what to build and why. A designer shapes interactions and structure. Developers implement behaviour. Testers investigate whether it meets expectations. Operations or reliability work keeps the released service running. Security responsibilities cut across these activities. Larger teams distribute the roles; an independent builder may switch between all of them in one afternoon.

The role names help you notice neglected work, not create unnecessary bureaucracy. Before release, ask which perspective you have not used. Have you prioritised like a product owner, tried the interface like a new user, checked failures like a tester, and considered recovery like an operator? AI assistance does not automatically supply these perspectives just because it produced many files.

sections.heading: Use AI inside a controlled loop
paragraphs: Give an assistant a bounded goal, relevant context, and a way to judge success. Ask for a plan when a change crosses several components. After implementation, inspect the change, run appropriate checks, and compare the actual behaviour with acceptance criteria. Keep the human approval point clear, especially for releases and destructive data operations.

For a small task feature, the loop can be short: clarify one rule, choose its design, implement it, test examples, release carefully, and gather feedback. You need not write a massive document at every stage. You do need evidence. When an assistant says the work is complete, ask what was tested, what remains uncertain, and what will happen if the released change fails.

chapters.keyIdea: Software development is a continuing learning loop, and generating code completes only one part of it.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard can release a small complete slice, such as task creation, before adding extra capabilities. The builder writes its criteria, designs validation and storage, reviews implementation, tests success and failure, then observes real use. Feedback can send the next change back to planning rather than straight into more code.

walkthrough.title: Run one lifecycle loop
steps: Plan a small task-creation improvement and record its purpose.
Design normal, invalid, and failed-save behaviour.
Implement the smallest coherent change and review its scope.
Test it against the criteria, including keyboard use and permissions.
Release with a recovery plan, gather feedback, and record the next learning.

mistakes: Equating a completed implementation with a completed release.
Treating accessibility, security, or maintenance as somebody else’s future problem.
aiMistakes: AI may announce completion after editing files without running checks; request the actual test results.
AI may remove a safeguard to make a demonstration pass; inspect the diff and repeat the failure case.
tryIt: Map a recent application change onto all six stages and mark any missing work.
Write a definition of done that covers correctness, accessibility, security, and maintainability.

check.q: What are the six recurring stages?
check.a: Planning, design, implementation, testing, release, and maintenance.

check.q: Who is accountable when a solo builder uses AI?
check.a: The builder remains responsible for the choices, verification, and released behaviour.

parts.title: Understanding How Applications Work
parts.question: What happens behind an interface when somebody uses an application?
parts.intro: Now follow information through the parts that make a feature work. You will learn to read small pieces of code, recognise trust boundaries, and investigate a real action using evidence.

project.title: Map and trace your application
project.summary: Draw the main components and trace one complete action between them. Mark the rules, persistent writes, and failure paths so the drawing becomes a practical review and debugging tool.
steps: Draw the user, browser frontend, backend, database, and external services.
Label connections with their protocols and the information they carry.
Trace task creation, sign-in, and retrieving tasks on a later visit.
Identify validation, session verification, ownership enforcement, and database constraints.
Capture one request in browser developer tools and compare it with the diagram.
Explain one failure at each boundary and how the user recovers.
Keep the diagram and traces with the application documentation and update them when behaviour changes.
